note.note:
Concise Clinical Note

Consult Summary:
- Telemedicine consult for acute, severe left-sided headache waking patient from sleep; working diagnosis is migraine, with stress and sleep deprivation as contributing factors.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Sudden onset, severe left-sided headache starting at ~5:30am, waking patient from sleep.
- Symptom timeline: Headache still present at consult, unresponsive to Paracetamol; history of previous milder, bilateral/frontally clustered headaches, but never one-sided or this severe.
- Associated symptoms: Mild photophobia (eye discomfort with light, tolerable), initial transient dizziness (resolved), no significant nausea or vomiting.
- Pertinent negatives: No neck stiffness, no fever, no visual disturbance, no neurological deficits reported, no family history of migraines.
- Past medical history: Anxiety, ongoing for ~2 years; no hypertension or other chronic disease.
- Medications: Sertraline (ongoing for anxiety); Paracetamol taken today with no benefit.
- Allergies: None known.
- Social/preventive: Lives with partner, non-smoker, runs ~3x/week, diet “OK,” not especially healthy or unhealthy, recent work-related stress and late nights, has a cat.

Examination:
- No physical examination performed (telemedicine context).
- No vital signs or neurological findings documented.
- No evidence of neck stiffness, photophobia requiring avoidance, or objective neuro or systemic signs discussed.

Impression:
- Working impression: Migraine (new, severe, unilateral headache with mild photophobia, prior headache history, recent stress/sleep deprivation).
  - Supported by: One-sided, severe pain; photophobia; previous headache history (though different character); recent stress/poor sleep; lack of systemic/neuro “red flag” findings.
- Alternative considerations: 
  - Tension-type headache (less likely—one-sided and severity atypical for tension; stress/anxiety relevant).
  - Secondary headache (e.g., intracranial mass) considered low likelihood; main warning feature is waking from sleep and new character, but lacks neurological deficits, vomiting, or chronicity.
  - Dehydration/sleep deprivation may be contributing, but too severe for sole explanation.
- Red flag review: No evidence for meningitis, encephalitis, cerebral venous sinus thrombosis, or subarachnoid hemorrhage given transcript details; will monitor and safety net.

Plan:
- Start Ibuprofen (higher dose if tolerated) as first-line for migraine; Paracetamol may be continued.
- Address possible triggers: advice to take time off work (self-certify for ~1 week if possible), consider counseling; link to self-referral counseling resources to be provided.
- Lifestyle recommendations: Ensure 7-8 hours sleep/night; maintain fluid intake of 1.5–2 liters water daily (excluding caffeine); monitor for signs of dehydration/fatigue.
- Safety net: Patient advised to review danger signs for headaches (education material to be provided); instructed to re-contact if symptoms worsen or new concerning symptoms develop.
- Follow-up: Scheduled telephone review in 1 week; advised possible further workup (bloods, other investigations) if no improvement.

Quality checks:

● Missing/expected elements:
  - No documented formal neurological examination (telemedicine limitations).
  - No vital signs recorded.
  - No blood pressure measurement (patient never had this checked).
  - Follow-up arranged; allergy/medication history obtained; social factors explored.
● Transcript vs DDx conflicts:
  - No major conflict; DDx concurs with transcript. No findings in transcript to support secondary causes (e.g., mass, thrombosis, meningitis); all discussed and safety-netted.
● Transcript quality:
  - Comprehensive history with systematic review of neurological red flags. Noisy at times but clinically adequate; missing objective examination (not possible remotely). Social, PMH, and medication histories are sufficient. Follow-up and safety netting clear.
